title: Seen the present, seen all
hook: whoever has seen the present has seen everything (Meditations 6.37)

segments.voice: Yesterday: letter by letter, the name spelled calmly and the duty done in order. Did you finish the first letter of that tangled task? Today closes the week, so we'll look back. Day five hundred eighty-one.

A complaint that a relative hasn't written. A request for money. Greetings to everyone at home. Those lines could come from this week's texts, and some readers find the same lines in letters that survive from the ancient world. Lovers' names scratched on a wall. Jokes. Insults. The costumes change. The scenes don't seem to. In book six, Marcus Aurelius draws a startling conclusion about time from exactly that sameness.
screen: `A REQUEST FOR MONEY.` → `LOVERS' NAMES ON A WALL.` → `THE SCENES DON'T CHANGE.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Meditations six, thirty-seven, in George Long's translation: "He who has seen present things has seen all." Marcus goes on: everything that has happened from eternity, and everything that will happen without end. Because, he says, all things are of one kin and one form. Second, what he means. Weddings, funerals, lawsuits, feasts, people flattering and people grieving. Marcus seems to think the play of human life runs on a small set of scenes, staged again and again with new actors. Look closely at the present, and you've seen the pattern of every age. Third, the Stoic background. Ancient writers report that the early Stoics taught the whole universe moves in great cycles, so history repeats in its shape. Not every reader today shares that picture of the cosmos, and Marcus himself sometimes holds it loosely. But you don't need the cosmology to feel the point. Fourth, why it matters. There are two ways to hear this line. One is weary: nothing's new, so why bother. The other is the way Marcus seems to mean it: the present is enough. You don't have to see the future to understand your life. You don't need the past to have been grander. On his reading, what there is to learn about being human is happening right in front of you, at this kitchen table, on this bus. So look. And this week, look back at what we've looked at. Back quickly. Stepmother and mother. In and out. Gymnasium. Show me I'm wrong. Letter by letter. Each one was a way of seeing the present clearly.
screen: `SEEN THE PRESENT, SEEN ALL.` · `THE SAME SCENES, NEW ACTORS.` · `THE STOIC CYCLES.` · `THE PRESENT IS ENOUGH.` · then, large: `SEEN IT ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your eyes rest on whatever is in front of you. Look at it closely, as if it were the only scene there has ever been. The light, the sounds, someone moving in the next room. People in Marcus's day sat in light like this, heard sounds like these, waited for someone they loved to come home. Stay with this moment, looking. The bell holds the time.
Seen the present. Marcus's claim that a close look at now shows you the pattern of every age. Today's word.
Your line: seen it all. Today, when you feel the pull of the past or the future, look closely at one ordinary scene in front of you instead, and say the line. Day five hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes use this line to steady themselves in the present, treating the ordinary scene in front of them as a full picture of human life rather than waiting for something new.

fork.setup: you feel your ordinary life is too small to teach you anything. what does Marcus's line suggest?
options: look closely at the present; the whole pattern is there.
fork.reveal: Meditations 6.37: he who has seen present things has seen all.

trapdoor: what you thought: a jaded line about nothing being new.
what it means: the present already holds the whole pattern of human life, so close attention to now is enough.
what a scholar hears: behind 6.37 sits the Stoic doctrine of cosmic cycles, in which the world is periodically consumed in fire and renewed in the same order.

notes: Editor review (y2 pass): removed both 'two thousand years' dates and the specific papyrus and graffiti claims (now 'some readers find'), softened 'many Stoics taught' to a report of the early Stoics, and the 'everything you need to learn' uplift; hook no longer invents Marcus watching the palace.
Confirm Long's wording of 6.37's opening clause, and the paraphrase of the rest ('of one kin and of one form').
Papyrus letters and Pompeii graffiti are described generally (Oxyrhynchus letters asking for money, greetings; lovers' names on walls). Confirm the 'nearly two thousand years ago' framing.
'Marcus himself sometimes holds it loosely' refers to his repeated 'either providence or atoms' alternatives; confirm the framing.
